subject: Chemistry
title: Francium: The Rarest Natural Element
description: Learn Francium: The Rarest Natural Element in one minute.

hook.text: At any given moment, there are fewer than 30 grams of francium on the entire Earth.

buildup.text: Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939 at the Curie Institute. She was the first woman to join the French Academy.

discovery.text: Francium forms when actinium decays, but it vanishes in about 22 minutes. It barely exists.

twist.text: Nobody has ever collected enough francium to see what it looks like. Its properties are mostly calculated.

climax.text: It's the most reactive metal—if you could gather enough, it would explode on contact with air.

punchline.text: Less than 30 grams on Earth. Gone in 22 minutes. Ghost metal.

quiz.question: Why has nobody seen a visible amount of francium?
options: It decays in about 22 minutes and barely exists naturally
It is invisible to the naked eye
It only exists inside the Sun

details.summary: Francium, discovered by Marguerite Perey in 1939, is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth, with only about 20 to 30 grams existing at any moment. It is so radioactive that its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of just 22 minutes, making it nearly impossible to study chemically.
details.whyItMatters: Francium demonstrates that the periodic table includes elements too unstable to accumulate in nature. Its properties are largely predicted from periodic trends rather than measured directly.
takeaways: Only about 20 to 30 grams of francium exist naturally on Earth at any moment
Its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of only 22 minutes
Marguerite Perey discovered it while working as Marie Curie's lab technician

faq.question: Why is francium so much rarer than other natural elements?
faq.answer: Francium forms briefly during the radioactive decay of actinium-227, but its own extreme radioactivity means it decays almost immediately. With a half-life of just 22 minutes, francium cannot accumulate. Any atom produced decays to radium or astatine long before significant quantities can build up.

faq.question: Has anyone ever seen or handled a bulk sample of francium?
faq.answer: No. No one has ever assembled enough francium atoms to see with the naked eye. At most, scientists have trapped a few hundred thousand atoms at a time using laser cooling techniques..
